meta.titre: Choose the correct verb form in a dialogue according to subject agreement and time markers

sections.contenu_markdown: In almost every grammar exercise on English exams, a single small word hidden in the sentence - "yesterday", "since", "already" - is the real key to the correct answer. Learning to spot these time markers turns a guessing game into a reliable method.

items: Subject-verb agreement in the present simple (he/she/it + verb+s)
Basic past tense forms of common irregular verbs (buy→bought, break→broke)

sections.contenu_markdown:
When choosing between several verb forms in brackets, two things must always be checked: (1) the SUBJECT of the sentence, for agreement (I/you/we/they + base form; he/she/it + verb+s in the present simple); (2) any TIME MARKER present in the sentence, which almost always fixes the tense to use.

Words like "yesterday", "last week", "two days ago" always require the simple past, never the present perfect. Words like "already", "just", "since", "for" (with a duration) usually require the present perfect instead. Reading the whole sentence for these clues, rather than guessing from the verb alone, is the reliable method.
sections.formule_principale: \text{time marker (yesterday, last week)} \Rightarrow \text{simple past} \quad;\quad \text{time marker (already, since, for)} \Rightarrow \text{present perfect}

sections.enonce_markdown: Complete: "She ……… (finish, finished, has finished) her homework two hours ago."

etapes.justification: The subject is "she", third person singular.
"two hours ago" is a precise past time marker.
etapes.resultat_markdown: "two hours ago" → requires the simple past

etapes.justification: A precise past time marker rules out the present perfect, even though the subject is third person singular.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The correct answer is "finished": the time marker "two hours ago" is precise, so the simple past is required, regardless of the fact that "has finished" might otherwise look tempting with a third-person subject.

items.erreur_markdown: Choosing the present perfect ("has broken") simply because the subject is third person singular, without checking the time marker.
items.pourquoi_faux: Subject agreement only tells you whether to add -s in the present simple; it says nothing about which TENSE to use. The time marker in the sentence, if present, always takes priority over any assumption based on the subject alone.
items.correction_markdown: Always scan the whole sentence for a time marker BEFORE deciding on the tense, even if the subject seems to suggest an obvious form.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the present perfect with a precise past time marker such as "yesterday" or "last week".
items.pourquoi_faux: The present perfect is used for past actions whose exact time is not stated; a precise time marker like "yesterday" is incompatible with it and always requires the simple past instead.
items.correction_markdown: Never combine the present perfect with a precise past time expression (yesterday, last week, in 2020...); use the simple past instead.

items.enonce_markdown: Complete: "They ……… (arrive, arrives, arrived) at school late this morning."
items.solution_markdown: arrived — "this morning" (a completed period) with a completed action calls for the simple past.

items.enonce_markdown: Complete: "My father ……… (work, works, has worked) for this company since 2015."
items.solution_markdown: has worked — "since 2015" indicates a duration continuing up to now, which requires the present perfect.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why "I have seen that film last week" is grammatically incorrect, and correct it.
items.solution_markdown: This sentence is incorrect because it combines the present perfect ("have seen") with a precise past time marker ("last week"), which is not allowed in standard English: the present perfect never takes a specific past time expression. The correct sentence is "I saw that film last week", using the simple past to match the precise time marker.

items_markdown: Check both the subject (for agreement) and any time marker (for tense) before choosing a verb form.
Precise past time markers (yesterday, last week, X days ago) always require the simple past.
Words like already, just, since, for (+duration) usually require the present perfect.
Never combine the present perfect with a precise past time expression.
